q: What is the best starting material for static link examination?
options: The received mail opened in a normal browser tab
An image of the employee's current shortcut to the message
The preserved artifact viewed through the approved tool
A forwarded description with the destination guessed from the label
explanation: The approved view preserves provenance and avoids ordinary interaction with content.

q: A security gateway fetches the destination seconds after receipt. What belongs in the interaction field?
options: The recipient clicked before their email application synced
Automated request observed; user action unknown
A user device submitted information to the destination immediately
The lack of browser telemetry proves the case involves no interaction
explanation: Scanner traffic is different evidence from a recipient action.

q: What should the analyst compare first for a misleading link label?
options: The displayed text and the recorded destination
The certificate expiry for the expected and observed services
The number of slashes in the two addresses shown
The email subject when it appears in two separate folders
explanation: The displayed text can differ from what the message actually references.

q: An offline parser cannot separate a malformed URL. What is a defensible record?
options: Assign the hostname from the longest familiar string in the address
Assume the link was never used because parsing failed
Replace the full value with a spelling supplied by the reporter
Preserve the original and mark parsing as unresolved
explanation: A parser failure is a limitation, and guessed fields weaken provenance.

q: Which part is the starting point for identifying a URL's destination operator?
options: The text before the URL in the email
The contents of a predictable query parameter
The parsed host or authority
The name of the requesting browser's process
explanation: The host identifies the destination being considered for independent verification.

q: A gateway rewrites links through a protective service. What should a reviewer preserve?
options: Just the public hostname of the organisation's rewrite service
The original and rewrite identities with source context
Only the rewritten field once it becomes searchable in the logs
The employee's recollection of the destination to replace the recorded URI
explanation: Preserving both states helps interpret what the employee and gateway saw.

q: Why keep the raw path and query in restricted evidence?
options: They can contain recipient-specific or business identifiers
They are always cryptographically necessary to calculate file hashes
They reveal the author of the email even without trace records
They let every employee see the same version of the case
explanation: The raw value may expose sensitive data even in a simple link.

q: A file-type recogniser and the MIME label disagree. What should the case say?
options: Trust the sender's MIME label because it controls message encoding
Discard the metadata mismatch if the attachment has the expected name
Label the document harmless if the file classifier returns a generic container
Record both observations and request review of the file structure
explanation: The label and byte-oriented classifier measure different aspects of the object.

q: What can a SHA-256 match support during case grouping?
options: The two attachments were opened by their recipients at the same time
The sender of both messages had permission to use that From address
Two collected byte streams match the same digest
The copied filenames are the ones that originally appeared in both messages
explanation: An exact byte match is useful for grouping while provenance remains separate.

q: A file is absent in internal hash lookups. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: The file is benign even though the reputation system has no entry
No matching record was found in those lookups
The file is definitely new to every recipient in the organisation
The attachment's MIME label must be incorrect for this format
explanation: Lookup coverage and history bound the meaning of a negative result.

q: What should an analyst record for a reputation lookup?
options: The result, source, timestamp and queried value
The result copied into the final ticket without the service's name
An indicator score unqualified by date or input value
The analyst's confidence without any details of the search
explanation: A traceable entry lets a reviewer assess relevance and freshness.

q: A screenshot names an archive but the actual bytes are unavailable. What can be recorded?
options: The file digest calculated from the visible characters of its name
The attachment type as if confirmed by static analysis
The result of an attachment scan run against a different file
The visible name and the missing inspection evidence
explanation: The screenshot can support a reported name, not byte-level findings.

q: What is the safest way to verify an unfamiliar invoice portal?
options: Follow the message's own help link and ask for their usual hostname
Ask the employee to re-open the page on the device used originally
Check with an approved owner through a known channel
Compare the company name in the URL with the subject of the email
explanation: Independent business verification avoids relying on information supplied by the message.

q: An employee confirms entering a work password while the attachment is still unclassified. What takes priority?
options: A complete malware verdict before the identity team is informed
Prompt identity handoff on the reported exposure
A second test of the same page using the employee's work credentials
A final classification of every related email before isolating the case
explanation: Identity risk can justify action while the artifact investigation continues.

q: A DNS request and no browser session event are available. What can the analyst say?
options: The name was looked up; user navigation remains unverified
The address was visited by the employee named in the original mail
The request confirms the exact document and query fields retrieved
The DNS request proves no user entered any information on the page
explanation: A name lookup has limited specificity about a user's actions.

q: How should an approved redacted link view be labeled?
options: As the original even after omission of the query and path
As a final externally shareable record without further review
As a replacement for the underlying evidence in the case system
As a derivative referencing the preserved evidence ID
explanation: A derivative must stay traceable to the original record.

q: A file was found in an archive by an approved workflow. How should its digest be recorded?
options: Keep only the archive hash and assign it to every child item
Apply the extracted file's digest to the original message instead
Give the extracted item its own digest and source reference
Use the most recent filename as the identifier for every copy
explanation: Each object has its own bytes and an extraction relationship worth preserving.

q: Which filename finding warrants cautious follow-up rather than a verdict?
options: The file has already been confirmed to be the required internal report
The name resembles a routine invoice but is unexpected
The business owner independently confirmed the exact authorized delivery
Trusted gateway evidence shows the item was held before delivery
explanation: An unexpected artifact needs verification without implying that compromise occurred.

q: The user says they opened the attachment. Endpoint telemetry shows a later process start. What should be assessed next?
options: Whether the process evidence actually links to the attachment
Whether the alert's time can be replaced with the recipient's estimate
Whether the file name alone establishes the process's malicious nature
Whether the user remembers exactly which technical process was created
explanation: A time sequence is useful, but causality needs corroborating evidence.

q: Why should the original email be preserved before derivation?
options: It ensures the displayed link must always match the raw destination
It makes other telemetry unnecessary for decisions about user exposure
It allows the analyst to omit source identifiers from their notes
It remains available for provenance and later review
explanation: A stable source lets multiple investigations reproduce observations.

q: A container is encrypted and policy forbids opening it through the standard viewer. What is the right handoff?
options: Open the container in the regular workstation tool to test its contents
Report all contents as inspected on the strength of the container type
Route preserved evidence and its current limits to the specialist
Delete the encrypted object because the initial static workflow cannot inspect it
explanation: The authorised specialist can decide what further work is permitted.

q: What does an ordinary file extension establish on its own?
options: That every byte conforms to the claimed application format
How the name presents the file's expected type
Whether the object can be delivered by a mail gateway
Whether the application opened the file in the recipient's session
explanation: A naming convention does not authenticate the underlying file structure.

q: A destination looks unusual, but a trusted owner confirms it serves an approved workflow. What should be retained?
options: The original discrepancy and the independent verification
Only the original suspicion so the case status cannot change later
The employee's approval of the unfamiliar site in place of service ownership
The label shown in the message as proof that all activity was benign
explanation: Document the new evidence and how it affected the current assessment.

q: Which handoff is most useful when artifact classification remains uncertain?
options: A screenshot with no case identifier or indication of the source
The attachment resent to an analyst's ordinary email account
A note saying investigation continues without a specific next action
Evidence pointer, uncertainty, proposed check and owner
explanation: An owned next check keeps an uncertain case actionable.

q: Which change most clearly shifts a case toward endpoint investigation?
options: The email sender changed the spelling of a department name
A second user reported an identical subject without opening it
A documented process event on the relevant workstation
The gateway labeled the attachment with a generic media type
explanation: An observed process changes the evidence about possible device activity.
